lessons.title: The lactation cycle
lessons.html:
The cow's year

Dairy production follows the cow's reproductive cycle. A cow calves, milks for a lactation, is dried off, rests, and calves again. The farm plans everything around this cycle.

The lactation curve

After calving, milk yield rises quickly to a peak in the first one to two months, then slowly declines until the cow is dried off. A cow with a higher peak usually gives more milk over the whole lactation, so good early-lactation management pays off for months.

StageWhat happensManagement focus
Early lactationYield rises to peak; cow loses body condition because intake lags behind milk demandFresh cow checks, high-quality feed, heat detection
Mid lactationYield slowly falls; cow should be pregnantMaintain intake, confirm pregnancy
Late lactationYield lower; cow regains conditionAvoid getting cows fat
Dry periodNo milking; udder rests and regenerates before next calvingDry cow therapy as prescribed, transition feeding

Calving interval

The calving interval is the time between two calvings. A shorter interval means cows spend more of their life in the high-yield part of the curve. To achieve the farm's target, a cow must get pregnant within a few months after calving. Missed heats and poor conception lengthen the interval and reduce income.

Milk composition

Milk is mostly water, with fat, protein, lactose and minerals. Fat and protein levels depend on breed (Jerseys higher than Holsteins), feeding, stage of lactation and health. Many milk buyers pay for fat and protein, so composition affects income as well as volume.

lessons.title: Breeding and genetics
lessons.html:
Getting cows pregnant

The cow's oestrous cycle is about three weeks. She shows heat for a short period, and ovulation follows. Insemination must be timed in relation to heat to give the best chance of conception.

Breeding methods

  • Artificial insemination (AI): semen from proven bulls is used by trained technicians. AI gives access to top genetics, reduces disease spread and removes the danger of keeping many bulls.
  • Natural service: bulls are used, often as follow-up after AI. Bulls must be fertility tested and disease free, and handled with care.
  • Synchronisation programmes: hormone programmes set up by the vet to control timing of heat and ovulation.

Measures of fertility

  • Heat detection rate: share of cows seen on heat when they should be.
  • Conception rate: share of services that result in pregnancy.
  • Services per conception.
  • Days to first service and calving interval.

Genetic improvement

Each cow's milk production depends on her genes and her environment (feeding, health, comfort). Genetics are improved by choosing bulls with good breeding values for the traits the farm needs: milk volume, fat and protein, udder conformation, fertility, longevity, health traits and calving ease. Records from milk recording and breed societies make this possible.

Crossbreeding, for example Jersey and Holstein, can improve fertility and health through hybrid vigour. Avoid inbreeding by not using bulls related to the cows.

Sexed semen

Sexed semen gives mostly heifer calves. It is often used on heifers to produce replacements and is more expensive.

Good fertility depends on teamwork: milkers who report heats, feeders who keep body condition right, the AI technician, and the vet. Records link all of these and show where the breeding programme is losing cows.

lessons.title: Herd structure, replacements and culling
lessons.html:
Keeping the herd productive

A dairy herd is a mix of cows in milk, dry cows, heifers of different ages and calves. The manager plans this structure so that enough heifers enter the herd each year to replace the cows that leave.

Replacement rate

Cows leave the herd because of low yield, infertility, mastitis, lameness, injury, age or death. The share of the herd replaced each year is the replacement rate. A high rate means high rearing costs; a very low rate can mean old, less productive cows are kept too long.

Culling decisions

Culling should be planned, not forced by emergencies. Common reasons, in order of what the farm can control:

  1. Infertility: cow not pregnant after repeated services.
  2. Chronic mastitis: repeated cases or high cell count.
  3. Chronic lameness.
  4. Low production compared with herd mates.
  5. Poor temperament or udder conformation.

Cull cows must be fit to transport and must not be sent for slaughter during a medicine withdrawal period. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 applies to slaughter for human consumption.

Cow comfort and production

Cows produce best when they are comfortable: enough lying time on soft, dry surfaces, shade and cooling in hot weather, good walkways, enough feed and water space and calm handling. Heat stress lowers intake, yield and fertility. Shade, sprinklers and fans can reduce it.

Measuring herd performance

  • Litres per cow per day and per lactation.
  • Fat and protein yield.
  • Calving interval and pregnancy rate.
  • Somatic cell count and mastitis cases.
  • Replacement and death rates.

Key points

  • Yield rises to a peak after calving and then declines; a higher peak means more milk.
  • A short calving interval keeps cows in the productive part of the curve.
  • AI with good bulls improves genetics; bulls must be handled carefully.
  • Plan culling around fertility, mastitis, lameness and production.
  • Cow comfort and cooling support yield and fertility.
